title: White House ‘Super Intelligence’ Task Force to hold its first meeting
key_facts: The White House AI task force formally adopted its charter after its first official meeting on Thursday 15 Oct 2026, starting a 120-day window to answer questions on AI policy.

It will commission a report from the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology on AI risk in three areas: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability.

A working group will implement the White House Accord on Super Intelligence signed this month by major AI CEOs, led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton (task force chair) with National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.
Defense Undersecretary Emil Michael, a vice chair, will lead protocols for labs to tell the government about breaches and cyber incidents.
A law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee including the Justice Department and FTC will be led by FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, also a vice chair.
Vice chair Scott Kupor, Director of the Office of Personnel Management, will work on critical infrastructure protection and, with the Labor Department, on AI's impact on the workforce.
How compliance will be enforced is unclear; a White House official said export controls could be one lever.
quote_evidence: The White House's AI task force has formally adopted its charter, kicking off the short 120-day window it's been given to answer some extremely thorny questions about how the government should handle the rapid development of AI technology.
It's not yet entirely clear how compliance with the task force will be enforced or how current law may apply to companies who don't adhere to the new protocols.
why_it_matters_hint: The task force now has a charter, a deadline and a defined risk agenda.
notes: Politico page (the item in the pool, written before the meeting) blocked (403); Semafor reports the outcome of the meeting from an announcement shared first with it.
